```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# Data ---------------------------------
frogs <- read.csv("../../data/ReedfrogSizepred.csv")
mn <- aggregate(Kill ~ TBL, data = frogs, FUN = mean)

ricker <- function(x, a, b) a * x * exp(-b * x)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines) for equation manipulation /
# show-your-work; pair with fig.height set to however much room is needed
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}
```

```{r key-helpers, include=FALSE}
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
# redraws blank_table() so cells flagged TRUE in `ans` use the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    font = if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}
```

```{r key-values, include=FALSE}
f2 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 2)
avals <- seq(0.1, 3, by = 0.05)
bvals <- seq(0.02, 0.40, by = 0.01)
ssr_grid <- outer(avals, bvals, Vectorize(function(a, b) sum((mn$Kill - ricker(mn$TBL, a, b))^2)))
best_idx <- which(ssr_grid == min(ssr_grid), arr.ind = TRUE)
a_best <- avals[best_idx[1, 1]]
b_best <- bvals[best_idx[1, 2]]
ssr_best <- min(ssr_grid)
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta.}


## Picking up where we left off

Last week (Act 3) you tried a few guesses for the $(a, b)$ parameters of the Ricker function by hand, recorded each one's SSR in a table, and tried to find a combination that best fit the tadpole data. That approach works, but it only samples a few scattered points out of a huge space of possible parameter combinations -- there could easily be a much better combination nobody in the room happened to try.

Today we replace guess-and-check with **grid search**: an algorithm that computes SSR at every combination of $a$ and $b$ across a fine grid, and picks out the best one automatically. This is a preview of something you'll do again in a few weeks -- once we replace "sum of squared residuals" with "likelihood".

**Before you do anything else: close your laptop and put your phone away.** Part 1 and the group check-in that follows are pen-and-paper only.

## Part 1: Plan the search (individual, ~15 min)

**1a. Propose a search range.** Based on last week's guesses, propose a reasonable range to search over for $a$ and for $b$ (order-of-magnitude is fine -- you're not committing to anything precise just yet):

$a$ from \ans{0 (any range that brackets last week's guesses is fine, e.g. $a$ from 0 to 3)} to \ans{3} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; $b$ from \ans{0} to \ans{0.5}

Roughly how many $(a,b)$ combinations would that range contain if you checked every $0.05$ for $a$ and every $0.01$ for $b$ (a rough estimate is fine)? \ans{a few thousand (the official range below has `r format(length(avals) * length(bvals), big.mark = ",")`)}

That's a lot of predictions and SSR calculations to run by hand. This is a job for a computer, not a pencil.

**1b. Design the algorithm.** Working from your range in 1a, write out (in plain English) the algorithm you'd need to check every combination of $a$ and $b$ and find the best one. Don't write R code; describe the procedure the way you'd explain it to someone who has never programmed. Think about: what you need to keep track of as you go, what gets recomputed at every single combination, and how you identify the winner once you've checked them all.

\ans{Make a list of candidate $a$ values and a list of candidate $b$ values, and a table to store one SSR per $(a, b)$ combination. For every combination: compute the Ricker prediction at each of the five tank sizes, subtract from the observed means, square, and sum to get the SSR; store it. When every combination has been checked, find the smallest stored SSR and report the $(a, b)$ that produced it.}

## Part 2B: Self-coded path (laptops, ~15-20 min)

Use the official search range for the rest of today's lab: $a =$ `seq(0.1, 3, by = 0.05)`, $b =$ `seq(0.02, 0.40, by = 0.01)`.

Translate your group's pseudocode into working R code yourselves (R's built-in help, documentation, stackOverflow and other human-generated websites, and your neighbors are fair game; AI tools are not). Run the grid search, find the best-fit $(a,b)$ and its SSR, and produce a heatmap or contour plot of the SSR surface (`image()` or `contour()` both work well).

\ansbegin

```{r ans-grid-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, highlight=FALSE}
avals <- seq(0.1, 3, by = 0.05)
bvals <- seq(0.02, 0.40, by = 0.01)
ssr_grid <- matrix(NA, length(avals), length(bvals))
for (i in seq_along(avals)) {
  for (j in seq_along(bvals)) {
    pred <- ricker(mn$TBL, avals[i], bvals[j])
    ssr_grid[i, j] <- sum((mn$Kill - pred)^2)
  }
}
best <- which(ssr_grid == min(ssr_grid), arr.ind = TRUE)
c(avals[best[1]], bvals[best[2]], min(ssr_grid))
image(avals, bvals, log(ssr_grid))
contour(avals, bvals, log(ssr_grid), add = TRUE)
```

\ansend

**Results.** Best-fit $a=$ \ans{`r a_best`} &nbsp;&nbsp; $b=$ \ans{`r b_best`} &nbsp;&nbsp; SSR $=$ \ans{`r f2(ssr_best)`}

Look at the heatmap/contour plot. Is the minimum comfortably inside your search range, or pinned against an edge? (If it's at an edge, that's a sign the range needs to extend further.)

\ans{Comfortably inside the range (see the closed contour around the $\times$).}

```{r ans-heatmap, fig.width=5, fig.height=3.6}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
image(avals, bvals, log(ssr_grid), col = hcl.colors(30, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
      xlab = "a", ylab = "b")
contour(avals, bvals, log(ssr_grid), add = TRUE, nlevels = 12)
points(a_best, b_best, pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 2, col = ans_col)
```
